title: Charting circumstellar chemistry of carbon-rich asymptotic giant branch stars. III. SiO and SiS abundances
comment: 14 pages, with 10 figures and 3 tables in the main text. Two appendices contain additional figures and tables. Total 22 pages. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: The present understanding of C-rich AGB chemistry largely relies on observations of the archetypal carbon star IRC+10216. Current molecular abundance estimates for carbon stars are based either on single-dish spectra sampling a range of excitation conditions, or on interferometric mapping of a few lines. We aim to estimate the circumstellar abundances of SiO, SiS, and their most abundant isotopologues ($^{29}$SiO, $^{30}$SiO, $^{29}$SiS, $^{30}$SiS, and Si$^{34}$S) for a sample of five carbon stars. We derived molecular abundances using detailed 1D non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) radiative transfer (RT) modelling, constrained by both morphological and excitation information obtained from spatially resolved ALMA maps and single-dish observations. We further compared the derived abundances to chemical modelling results. We obtain good fits to the SiO and SiS line profiles, and derived well-constrained abundance profiles and reliable isotopic ratios for all sources except AFGL 3068. While the SiS peak abundances are very similar across the sample (2.0$\times$10$^{-6}-4.7\times$10$^{-6}$), we find that the SiO peak abundances of the rest of the stars are a factor of $\sim$5 larger than that of IRC+10216. The $e$-folding radii ($R_\mathrm{e}$) are in the range 1.3$\times$10$^{16}-7.0\times$10$^{16}$ cm for SiO and 6.0$\times$10$^{15}-1.0\times$10$^{17}$ cm for SiS. The $R_\mathrm{e}$ increases with gas density for both SiO and SiS. Chemical models reproduce the derived SiO abundance profiles well, while over-predicting the SiS $R_\mathrm{e}$ values. Our models highlight the necessity of having spatially resolved observations across a broad range of excitation conditions, while also making evident the limitations inherent in 1D RT modelling using simplified (circum)stellar models. We find that the currently assumed SiS photodissociation rate in chemical models is underestimated.

AI.tldr: This paper derives circumstellar abundances of SiO, SiS, and their isotopologues for five carbon stars using 1D non-LTE radiative transfer modeling constrained by ALMA and single-dish observations. SiO peak abundances vary by ~5× across the sample, while SiS abundances are similar. Chemical models reproduce SiO but overpredict SiS e-folding radii, suggesting the SiS photodissociation rate is underestimated.
AI.motivation: Current understanding of C-rich AGB chemistry relies heavily on IRC+10216, and existing molecular abundance estimates are based either on single-dish spectra or limited interferometric mapping. This work aims to estimate circumstellar abundances of Si-bearing molecules (SiO, SiS, and isotopologues) for a broader sample of five carbon stars to improve generalizability.
AI.method: Detailed 1D non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (non-LTE) radiative transfer (RT) modeling, constrained by both morphological and excitation information from spatially resolved ALMA maps and single-dish observations. Derived abundances were compared to chemical modeling results.
AI.result: Good fits to SiO and SiS line profiles; well-constrained abundances for all sources except AFGL 3068. SiS peak abundances similar across sample (2.0×10⁻⁶–4.7×10⁻⁶), but SiO peak abundances vary by ~5×. e-folding radii range: SiO 1.3×10¹⁶–7.0×10¹⁶ cm; SiS 6.0×10¹⁵–1.0×10¹⁷ cm, increasing with gas density. Chemical models reproduce SiO profiles but overpredict SiS Rₑ values.
AI.conclusion: Spatially resolved observations across broad excitation conditions are necessary. 1D RT modeling with simplified stellar models has inherent limitations. The currently assumed SiS photodissociation rate in chemical models is likely underestimated.

title: The Nova Synthetic Data Base: A Principal Component/AI Analysis of Novae Synoptic Spectra
comment: 15 pages (ApJ style), 3 figures, 13 tables. Matches the published version in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series. Nova Synthetic Data Base (NSDB) available at http://specmodels.iag.usp.br. Includes an extensive Appendix with 7 tables of spectral-space selection
summary: The Nova Synthetic Data Base (NSDB) is presented as the first publicly available database of synthetic spectra for classical nova shells, spanning an unprecedented range of physical parameters (e.g., ejecta mass, chemical composition, temperature, and luminosity of the white dwarf) at several post-eruption ages. Generated using detailed 3D photoionization models, this homogeneous database enables a systematic exploration of spectral features in novae. In this work, we introduce a principal component analysis/AI-based framework to derive time-dependent proxies for retrieving the physical properties of novae from limited spectral data. By analyzing the correlations between the eigenspectra and the grid's variables, a reduced set of diagnostic spectral lines is derived, paving the way for robust multiregressor machine-learning algorithms with a minimal effort observational set. The prediction capability of the method is high and robust to data noise. The results establish a proof of concept for the use of model grids combined with physically controlled AI as a tool to interpret novae observations in the context of the large number of events expected from future wide-area surveys.

AI.tldr: NSDB is the first public synthetic spectra database for classical nova shells, covering a wide range of physical parameters. The authors introduce a PCA/AI framework to derive time-dependent proxies for retrieving physical properties from limited spectral data, achieving high and noise-robust prediction capability, establishing a proof of concept for model grids + physically controlled AI for future surveys.
AI.motivation: To create the first publicly available synthetic spectra database for classical nova shells with broad physical parameter coverage, and to develop a method for efficiently retrieving physical properties from limited spectral observations, in preparation for the large number of events expected from future wide-area surveys.
AI.method: Generated homogeneous database using detailed 3D photoionization models (NSDB); applied principal component analysis and AI-based framework to derive time-dependent proxies; used eigenspectra analysis to identify a reduced set of diagnostic spectral lines; implemented multiregressor machine-learning algorithms.
AI.result: High prediction capability robust to data noise; a reduced set of diagnostic spectral lines identified; proof of concept for combining model grids with physically controlled AI for nova interpretation.
AI.conclusion: The NSDB combined with PCA/AI framework enables efficient retrieval of nova physical properties from limited spectral data, demonstrating potential for interpreting the large number of nova events expected from future surveys.

title: Rotationally modulated highly circularly polarised radio pulses from the rapidly rotating M dwarf ASKAP J181335-604720
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters
summary: We report the detection of strong, highly circularly polarised, and rotationally modulated radio pulses from the early-mid M dwarf ASKAP J181335-604720, based on strictly simultaneous radio and optical observations with the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). The ASKAP data reveal recurrent broadband radio pulses across 800-1088 MHz, with peak circular polarisation fractions approaching 100%. A dominant period of P = 5.607 +- 0.003 h is derived from the TESS light curve using a Lomb-Scargle analysis, which we interpret as the stellar rotation period. When phase-folded on this period, the radio emission is confined to narrow phase intervals and recurs at fixed rotational phases, consisting of a dominant pulse and a weaker secondary component. No contemporaneous optical flares are detected at the epochs of the radio pulses in the simultaneous TESS data. Even under conservative assumptions, the inferred brightness temperature exceeds Tb > 1.8 * 10^12 K, ruling out incoherent emission mechanisms. Combining the observed characteristics, we interpret the emission as coherent electron cyclotron maser (ECM) radiation arising from the stellar magnetosphere, with the observed frequencies implying local magnetic field strengths of at least several hundred Gauss in the radio-emitting region. This work provides a clean, well-constrained, and strictly simultaneous radio-optical case, demonstrating that coordinated radio and optical observations offer a powerful means of distinguishing magnetospheric coherent radio emission from flare-associated coronal activity in M dwarfs.

AI.tldr: ASKAP J181335-604720, an early-mid M dwarf, exhibits strongly circularly polarized, rotationally modulated radio pulses (800-1088 MHz) with ~100% circular polarization, a 5.607 h rotation period (from TESS), brightness temperature >1.8×10^12 K, and no coincident optical flares, consistent with electron cyclotron maser (ECM) emission from the stellar magnetosphere at ~several hundred Gauss field strengths.
AI.motivation: To detect and characterize coherent radio emission from M dwarfs and distinguish magnetospheric ECM radiation from flare-associated coronal activity using strictly simultaneous radio (ASKAP) and optical (TESS) observations.
AI.method: Strictly simultaneous ASKAP (800-1088 MHz) and TESS observations; Lomb-Scargle period analysis of TESS light curve to determine rotation period; phase-folding of radio data; brightness temperature calculation; comparison of radio pulse timing with optical flare activity.
AI.result: Strong, highly circularly polarized (~100%) broadband radio pulses detected; rotation period P=5.607±0.003 h identified; radio emission confined to narrow phase intervals at fixed rotational phases; no simultaneous optical flares; Tb > 1.8×10^12 K; inferred magnetic field strength ≥ several hundred Gauss in the emitting region.
AI.conclusion: The emission is coherent ECM radiation from the stellar magnetosphere, not flare-associated coronal activity. Coordinated radio-optical observations effectively distinguish magnetospheric from coronal emission mechanisms in M dwarfs.

title: On the quenching of LRD X-ray emission by both Compton-thick gas and high accretion rates
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, submitted. Comments are welcome
summary: Little Red Dots (LRDs), candidate high-redshift supermassive black holes accreting in dense gas, remain undetected in X-rays. In previous work, we provided the first quantitative models that reproduce the optical and near-infrared spectra of LRDs with the Sirocco radiative transfer code, thereby constraining the properties of the surrounding gas. Here, we use those constraints to predict the X-ray attenuation produced by dense gas cocoons, and explore its dependence on Balmer-break strength, metallicity, intrinsic X-ray SED, and observed bandpass as a function of redshift. We find that the X-ray constraints are very tight, requiring both extinction by a Compton-thick gas column $N_{\rm H}\sim10^{25}\,{\rm cm}^{-2}$ with moderate metallicity ($0.05$-$0.1\,Z_\odot$) and intrinsically weak X-ray emission (bolometric to X-ray luminosity ratio, $k_{\rm bol,X}\gtrsim 30$) as observed in high accretion rate, narrow-line AGN, to make LRDs sufficiently faint to evade detection. Intrinsically bright X-ray emitters as seen in typical broad-line AGN would be detected even behind the typical modest metallicity, Compton-thick gas columns inferred from the optical spectra. Very low metallicity objects could be detected in X-rays even with low intrinsic X-ray luminosities, suggesting that LRDs are not (currently) chemically pristine.

AI.tldr: Little Red Dots (LRDs) — candidate high-redshift supermassive black holes — remain X-ray undetected. Using radiative transfer models, this work predicts that they require both Compton-thick gas columns (NH~10^25 cm^-2) with moderate metallicity (0.05-0.1 Z⊙) and intrinsically weak X-ray emission (kbol,X≳30) to evade X-ray detection, ruling out intrinsically bright X-ray emitters and very low metallicity scenarios.
AI.motivation: Little Red Dots (LRDs) are candidate high-redshift supermassive black holes accreting in dense gas, but they remain undetected in X-rays. This work aims to explain why by modeling the X-ray attenuation from their surrounding gas cocoons.
AI.method: The authors use constraints on LRD gas properties derived from optical/NIR spectra modeled with the Sirocco radiative transfer code, then predict X-ray attenuation as a function of Balmer-break strength, metallicity, intrinsic X-ray SED, and redshift-dependent bandpass.
AI.result: X-ray non-detection requires both Compton-thick gas columns (NH~10^25 cm^-2) with moderate metallicity (0.05-0.1 Z⊙) and intrinsically weak X-ray emission (kbol,X≳30), similar to high accretion rate, narrow-line AGN. Typical broad-line AGN would be detectable even behind such columns, and very low metallicity objects would be detectable even with low intrinsic X-ray luminosity.
AI.conclusion: LRDs evade X-ray detection only under a combination of Compton-thick obscuration and intrinsically weak X-ray emission; they cannot have very low metallicity or bright intrinsic X-ray emission, implying they are not chemically pristine.

title: Mechanisms for magnetic braking boost and disruption: the role of irradiation-driven winds and convective turnover time spike in cataclysmic variables
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: The saturated, boosted, and disrupted magnetic braking (SBD MB) model is an empirical prescription that has recently gained support from close-binary observations. Different boosting ($K$) and disruption ($η$) parameters appear necessary for different systems, but their physical origins remain uncertain. We aim to identify the mechanisms that boost magnetic braking (MB) and cause its disruption at the fully convective boundary in cataclysmic variables (CVs). We modelled CV evolution with MESA and compared the results with observed CV properties. We computed the convective turnover time ($τ_c$) directly from the donor's structure rather than adopting empirical relations. We also included irradiation from the accreting white dwarf, which heats the donor's outer layers and can drive additional winds that enhance MB. The structure-based $τ_c$ calculation reveals a pronounced spike as the donor approaches full convection, which drives the disruption parameter $η$ and initiates the period gap in CVs. The outcome of irradiation is sensitive to the accretion, irradiation, and wind efficiencies, all of which are poorly constrained from observations. Despite these uncertainties, plausible parameter choices allow irradiation-driven winds to provide the required boost $K$ during accreting phases. We refer to the combined prescription as the i$τ$SBD MB model and find that it yields evolutionary tracks broadly consistent with the main CV properties. Our i$τ$SBD MB framework offers a physically motivated interpretation of the empirical boost and disruption factors in SBD MB for CV evolution. We suggest that the convective turnover time spike at the fully convective boundary may drive MB disruption for fast-rotating stars in the saturated regime, while irradiation-driven winds may be the dominant mechanism boosting MB in accreting binaries and other strongly irradiated close systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the iτSBD MB model, where a spike in convective turnover time at the fully convective boundary drives magnetic braking disruption (opening the CV period gap), and irradiation-driven winds from the accreting white dwarf provide the necessary boosting of magnetic braking, offering a physically motivated interpretation of the empirical SBD MB parameters.
AI.motivation: The empirical SBD MB model requires different boosting (K) and disruption (η) parameters for different systems, but their physical origins remain uncertain. This work aims to identify the mechanisms that boost MB and cause its disruption at the fully convective boundary in CVs.
AI.method: CV evolution was modeled with MESA, computing convective turnover time (τ_c) directly from the donor's structure instead of using empirical relations. Irradiation from the accreting white dwarf was included, heating the donor's outer layers and potentially driving additional winds that enhance MB.
AI.result: Structure-based τ_c reveals a pronounced spike as the donor approaches full convection, driving the disruption parameter η and initiating the period gap. Irradiation-driven winds can provide the required boost K during accreting phases with plausible parameter choices, though outcomes are sensitive to poorly constrained efficiencies.
AI.conclusion: The iτSBD MB framework offers a physically motivated interpretation of the empirical boost and disruption factors. The τ_c spike at the fully convective boundary may drive MB disruption for fast-rotating saturated stars, while irradiation-driven winds may be the dominant mechanism boosting MB in accreting binaries and strongly irradiated close systems.

title: Energy Evolution from the Chromosphere to the Heliosphere in the 2021 October 28 Solar Eruption
summary: We perform a detailed study of the energetics for a well-observed solar eruption and flare that occurred on 28 October 2021. This event included a GOES class X1.0 flare, a global EUV wave, and a coronal mass ejection that reached speeds of >2000 km/s. The event was observed from a variety of spacecraft in NASA's Heliophysics System Observatory, including multiple missions near Earth, STEREO-A off the Sun-Earth line, and Solar Orbiter, near the Sun-Earth line at about 0.8 au. Using remote sensing, in situ observations, and in some cases scaling laws based on previous observations, we characterize the following quantities: free magnetic energy, energy in non-thermal electrons, energy in non-thermal ions, bolometric energy, energy deposited in the chromosphere, thermal energy radiated in the flare loops, energy dissipated by the EUV wave, CME kinetic and gravitational potential energy, CME energy flux in the heliosphere, and the energy partition in the CME shock. We find that the total energy released during the event is consistent with estimates of the pre-event stored magnetic energy, and the CME kinetic + potential energy dominates the energy partition.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the energetics of a solar eruption (X1.0 flare, global EUV wave, and CME >2000 km/s) on 28 October 2021, using multi-spacecraft observations (NASA's HSO, STEREO-A, Solar Orbiter) and scaling laws. They quantify various energy components (magnetic, non-thermal electrons/ions, bolometric, chromospheric, thermal, EUV wave, CME kinetic/potential, CME shock energy flux) and find total released energy consistent with pre-event stored magnetic energy, with CME kinetic + potential energy dominating.
AI.motivation: To perform a comprehensive energy budget analysis of a well-observed major solar eruption to understand the partition of released energy among different components (flare, CME, waves, particles, radiation) and validate consistency with pre-event free magnetic energy estimates.
AI.method: Remote sensing and in situ observations from multiple spacecraft (near-Earth missions, STEREO-A, Solar Orbiter) combined with scaling laws from previous studies to estimate free magnetic energy, non-thermal electron/ion energy, bolometric energy, chromospheric deposition, thermal flare loop radiation, EUV wave dissipation, CME kinetic and gravitational potential energy, CME heliospheric energy flux, and CME shock energy partition.
AI.result: Total released energy is consistent with pre-event stored magnetic energy. The CME kinetic + potential energy dominates the overall energy partition of the event.
AI.conclusion: The energy budget of this X1.0 flare/CME event is closed within the uncertainty of pre-event magnetic free energy estimates, and the CME bulk motion (kinetic + potential) is the primary energy sink, exceeding flare-related radiative and particle components.

title: A stellar bar hidden in an extreme gas-rich disk galaxy at z=4.055
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ApJL
summary: The classical picture for the formation of stellar bars -- key dynamical drivers of the evolution of galaxies -- is through secular evolution of instability in gas poor, stellar-dominated disks. The detection with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) of stellar bars and spiral arms in galaxies at early cosmic times has thus challenged LambdaCDM-based expectations, which recent studies reconcile by suggesting that these galaxies are baryon-dominated and have already consumed most of their gas. Yet, a paradox arises, as early galaxies are expected to be increasingly rich in gas, which is generally considered to prevent or slow down stellar bar formation. Here, we show the detection of a stellar bar in GN20, a gas-rich star-forming disk galaxy at a redshift of z=4.055, only 1.5 billion years after the Big Bang. Simultaneous observations of the stars, gas, and dust reveal that GN20 is indeed baryon-dominated (over dark matter; 70+/-30%), but the baryonic mass is largely in the form of gas (75+/-25%). This discovery demonstrates that gas-rich disks do support rapid stellar bar formation in the early Universe, motivating a new theoretical perspective on bar formation in gas-rich systems, and providing a potential new mechanism for very early galaxy assembly and quenching.

AI.tldr: JWST detection of a stellar bar in GN20, a gas-rich galaxy at z=4.055, challenges the classical view that bars form only in gas-poor disks, showing that gas-rich, baryon-dominated galaxies can form bars rapidly in the early Universe.
AI.motivation: To resolve the paradox between JWST observations of stellar bars in early galaxies (which challenge LambdaCDM expectations) and the classical picture that gas-rich environments prevent bar formation, by investigating whether gas-rich disks can support bar formation at high redshift.
AI.method: Simultaneous JWST observations of stars, gas, and dust in GN20, a gas-rich star-forming disk galaxy at z=4.055, to measure its baryonic composition and detect a stellar bar.
AI.result: GN20 is baryon-dominated (70±30% over dark matter), but 75±25% of its baryonic mass is in gas. Despite being gas-rich, it hosts a stellar bar, proving gas-rich disks can support rapid bar formation in the early Universe.
AI.conclusion: This discovery challenges the classical secular evolution picture, motivates new theoretical models for bar formation in gas-rich systems, and suggests a potential new mechanism for very early galaxy assembly and quenching.

title: The Simulated Oxygen Shortage (SOS): Mapping the Missing OVI in Simulated Dwarf Galaxies to Subgrid Physics
summary: Observations reveal extended \OVI\, reservoirs in the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of dwarf galaxies, yet current simulations systematically underpredict \OVI\, column densities. Utilizing two suites run with different simulation codes, the \MM\, simulations (Marvelous Massive Dwarfs and Marvel-ous Dwarfs) and the publicly available FIRE-2 simulations, we explore the role of subgrid models and the resulting CGM phase in shaping \OVI\, production. By comparing observationally derived \OVI\, masses to the mass of oxygen produced over the galaxies' star formation history, we find evidence for an underproduction of oxygen for low-mass simulated galaxies. Despite clear differences in feedback implementation, CGM structure, and metal mixing, we find that \OVI\, in both suites generally self-selects cool/warm ($\rm log\, T\,/K \sim 4.5$), diffuse ($\rm log\,n_{gas}\,/cm^{-3} \sim -5.0 $), and moderately metal-enriched ($\rm log\, Z/Z_{\odot} \sim -1 $) material at large radii from the galaxy. We show that neither the choice of ultraviolet background nor plausible variations in CGM thermal structure can close the gap with observations. Taken together, our results point to a possible underproduction of oxygen in low-mass galaxies. Feedback prescriptions contribute via insufficient metal transport to large radii. Hence, the \OVI\, deficit may motivate an investigation of current modeling choices for supernova yields, star formation, and feedback in low-metallicity environments.

AI.tldr: Current simulations underpredict OVI column densities in the CGM of dwarf galaxies. By analyzing two simulation suites (MM and FIRE-2), the study finds evidence for oxygen underproduction in low-mass simulated galaxies, with OVI residing in cool/warm, diffuse, moderately metal-enriched gas at large radii. Neither UV background nor CGM thermal structure variations can explain the gap with observations, pointing to insufficient oxygen production and inadequate metal transport from feedback prescriptions.
AI.motivation: To understand why current simulations systematically underpredict OVI column densities in the CGM of dwarf galaxies, despite observations revealing extended OVI reservoirs.
AI.method: Comparison of two simulation suites (MM and FIRE-2) with different subgrid models and feedback implementations, analyzing OVI masses relative to oxygen produced over star formation history, and examining CGM phase properties of OVI-bearing gas.
AI.result: OVI self-selects cool/warm (log T/K ~ 4.5), diffuse (log n_gas/cm^-3 ~ -5.0), moderately metal-enriched (log Z/Z_sun ~ -1) gas at large radii. Evidence for oxygen underproduction in low-mass galaxies; neither UV background nor CGM thermal structure variations can close the gap with observations.
AI.conclusion: The OVI deficit likely stems from underproduction of oxygen in low-mass galaxies and insufficient metal transport to large radii due to feedback prescriptions, motivating reinvestigation of supernova yields, star formation, and feedback modeling in low-metallicity environments.

title: Witnessing the rapid growth of disk galaxies over cosmic time using JWST and HST
comment: 17 pages, 5 figure. Accepted for publication in A&A. Comments are welcome. Samaneraji@gmail.com
summary: Measuring galaxy sizes is fundamental to understanding how galaxies grow and evolve. Traditional methods to measure sizes either trace the concentration of light (i.e., effective radius) or are limited by the depth of the survey (isophotal methods). With the advent of deep, wide surveys, a new physically motivated definition of size has emerged: the edge of the galaxy, defined as the most distant location where star formation has occurred or is still occurring. In this work, we take advantage of the extraordinary depth and spatial resolution of the Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes to perform an accurate study of galaxy edges at $z=1$. Using 22 photometric bands, we derive radial age and metallicity profiles for two disk galaxies in the GOODS-South field with stellar masses of around $4\times10^{10}\ M_\odot$. The age profiles display a characteristic U-shape, while the metallicity profiles steadily decrease with galactocentric distance. The turnover in the age profile occurs near the galaxy edge, suggesting that stellar migration is responsible for the stars beyond the edge of these galaxies. Comparison with $z=0$ disk galaxies suggests that galaxies at $z=1$ grow inside-out, with little or no increase in mass within the inner 8 kpc, but a significant increase (approximately 300\%) in the outer regions.

AI.tldr: Using HST and JWST data, this study measures the radial age and metallicity profiles of two z=1 disk galaxies, revealing U-shaped age profiles and declining metallicity profiles. The age turnover near the galaxy edge suggests stellar migration, and comparison to local galaxies indicates inside-out growth with ~300% mass increase in outer regions but little change within 8 kpc.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations of traditional galaxy size measurement methods (effective radius and isophotal methods) by using a new physically motivated definition—the galaxy edge—and to understand galaxy growth at z=1 using deep, high-resolution multi-wavelength data.
AI.method: Analyzed two disk galaxies in GOODS-South (M* ~ 4×10^10 M⊙) at z=1 using 22 photometric bands from HST and JWST to derive radial age and metallicity profiles.
AI.result: Age profiles show a characteristic U-shape; metallicity profiles decrease with radius. The age turnover coincides with the galaxy edge. Compared to z=0 disks, mass inside 8 kpc remains nearly unchanged, while outer regions show ~300% mass increase.
AI.conclusion: Galaxies at z=1 grow inside-out via stellar migration, with the galaxy edge marking a boundary where migration populates the outer stellar component.

title: Clumps in spiral galaxies at $z \lesssim 3$: Disentangling two spatial modes of star formation
comment: 20 pages, 21 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: At high redshifts, star formation in galaxies is more often concentrated in clumps than in spiral arms. Although clumps are actively studied, it is rarely done considering spiral arms as objects for study as well, and the connection between clumps and spirals remains understudied. We used a sample of 159 spiral galaxies at $0.1 \leq z \leq 3.3$ observed by HST and JWST. Using the residual images from photometric models with spiral arms constructed before, which was not done previously, we have done identification of clumps and measured their properties with photometric decomposition, finding 3003 clumps in overall, and performing SED fitting for a fraction of them. We examined the overall properties of clumps, focusing on the properties of spiral structure. We found that clumps luminosities, masses and sizes are smaller than commonly accepted in literature, either for the reason spiral arms were modelled separately, or because clumps in spiral galaxies are different compared to clumpy ones. We demonstrate the connection between clumps and spirals, in particular clumps are spatially concentrated towards spirals and various parameters of clumps and spirals correlate. Also, clumps in spiral arms tend to be smaller but brighter compared to clumps in inter-arm area, but their colours are similar. There are also some differences between clumps and spirals such as colour, emphasizing the importance of their separate analysis. Our results probably indicate that spiral arms stimulate the formation of clumps, although star formation properties of clumps in spiral arms is not changed compared to inter-arm region.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes 3003 clumps in 159 spiral galaxies at z=0.1-3.3 using HST/JWST data with photometric decomposition that accounts for spiral arms, finding clumps are smaller/less massive than previously reported and are spatially concentrated towards spiral arms.
AI.motivation: The connection between star-forming clumps and spiral arms at high redshift is understudied, as previous work rarely treats spiral arms as separate objects or considers their relationship with clumps.
AI.method: 159 spiral galaxies at 0.1≤z≤3.3 observed by HST and JWST; residual images from photometric models with spiral arms constructed beforehand; photometric decomposition to identify 3003 clumps; SED fitting for a fraction; analysis of clump properties focusing on spiral structure.
AI.result: Clump luminosities, masses, and sizes are smaller than commonly accepted; clumps are spatially concentrated towards spiral arms; clump and spiral parameters correlate; clumps in arms are smaller/brighter than inter-arm clumps but have similar colors.
AI.conclusion: Spiral arms likely stimulate clump formation, but star formation properties of clumps in arms versus inter-arm regions are not changed; separate analysis of clumps and spirals is important due to color differences.

title: A VLBA-resolved Jet Associated with Super-Eddington Accretion in a Radio-loud Quasar at $z=3.4$
summary: We report the detailed jet properties of eROSITA Final Equatorial Depth Survey (eFEDS) J084222.9+001000 (hereafter ID830), a radio-loud super-Eddington quasar at $z=3.4351$, revealed by Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) observations at 1.6 GHz, 4.9 GHz, and 8.2 GHz. Thanks to the high spatial resolution of the VLBA, we successfully resolve a parsec-scale core-jet structure of ID830, and find a well-collimated jet extending over $\approx 745$ pc, making it the most distant and one of the very few currently known radio-loud quasars with a resolved jet associated with super-Eddington accretion. The physical scale and evolutionary track of ID830 differs markedly from the low-$z$ analogues, such as nearby radio-luminous high-Eddington narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies, suggesting that this source represents a distinct high-$z$ population compared to previously known samples, with important implications for AGN feedback in early galaxy evolution. We also find that the jet has a relativistic speed of $v \gtrsim 0.19c$ and a modest viewing angle of $φ\lesssim 79^\circ$ to the line of sight, although its emission is not significantly Doppler-boosted ($δ\sim 1$). This provides the first evidence that such a relativistic and collimated jet can be produced over several hundred parsecs in the super-Eddington phase, lasting for at least $10^{3\text{-}4}$ yr. Our results call for further theoretical and numerical studies to understand the physical processes required to sustain such large-scale collimation in super-Eddington accretion, which remains a missing piece.

AI.tldr: This paper reports VLBA observations of a high-redshift (z=3.4351) radio-loud super-Eddington quasar (ID830) from the eROSITA eFEDS survey, resolving a parsec-scale relativistic jet extending ~745 pc—the most distant such object known. The jet has v ≥ 0.19c, viewing angle ≤79°, and no significant Doppler boosting, showing that super-Eddington accretion can sustain collimated relativistic jets over hundreds of parsecs for at least 10³⁻⁴ years, distinct from low-z analogues.
AI.motivation: To understand whether super-Eddington accretion can produce relativistic, collimated jets on parsec scales at high redshift, and to explore the implications for AGN feedback in early galaxy evolution, since such objects are extremely rare and poorly observed.
AI.method: VLBA observations at 1.6 GHz, 4.9 GHz, and 8.2 GHz to resolve the parsec-scale radio structure; multi-frequency imaging and spectral analysis to derive jet morphology, physical scale, speed, viewing angle, and Doppler factor.
AI.result: Resolved a core-jet structure extending ~745 pc; jet speed v ≥ 0.19c; viewing angle φ ≤ 79°; no significant Doppler boosting (δ ~ 1); the source differs markedly from low-z analogs like narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies, representing a distinct high-z population.
AI.conclusion: A relativistic, collimated jet can be produced and maintained over several hundred parsecs during the super-Eddington phase for at least 10³⁻⁴ yr. This challenges existing models and calls for further theoretical and numerical studies to explain large-scale collimation under super-Eddington accretion.

title: The Low-$α$ Splash Population in the Milky Way
comment: Submitted to AAS Journals. Comments are welcome!
summary: The Milky Way in-situ halo, also known as the Splash, consists of old (Age $>$ 10 Gyr), metal-rich ([Fe/H] $> -0.7$), high-$α$ stars, i.e., thick disk-like chemistry, on halo-like orbits (eccentricity > 0.6). Its origin is linked to stars formed in the disk and dynamically heated by either internal or external agents. In this work, we investigate its low-$α$ counterpart, the low-$α$ Splash, motivated by recent findings of an old thin disk population. We conjecture that any mechanism capable of heating disk stars should affect both of present-day high- and low-$α$ old populations. Using data from the APOGEE DR17 spectroscopic catalog, we identify metal-rich low-$α$ stars with halo-like kinematics similar to those of the classical high-$α$ Splash. We investigate their possible heating mechanisms using the GASTRO suite of simulations, which allows us to explore the effects of star-forming clumps as well as a major merger in the proto-disk of a Milky Way analog galaxy. Our main results show that only clumpy Milky Way models are able to produce Splash populations through scattering by clumps in the early Galaxy, including the low-$α$ counterpart, whereas the model including only the merger and without an early clumpy phase fails to produce these populations. In the models, the low-$α$ Splash corresponds to a subset of the old thin disk that was dynamically heated by the same mechanism responsible for the formation of the high-$α$ Splash.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a low-α counterpart to the Milky Way's in-situ halo (Splash) — metal-rich stars with halo-like orbits but low α abundances — and uses simulations (GASTRO) to show that only clumpy Milky Way models (not merger-only models) can produce both high-α and low-α Splash populations via dynamical heating of old disk stars.
AI.motivation: Recent findings of an old thin disk population motivated the search for a low-α counterpart to the classical high-α Splash, testing whether any heating mechanism affecting disk stars impacts both high- and low-α old populations.
AI.method: Data from APOGEE DR17 was used to identify metal-rich low-α stars with halo-like kinematics; the GASTRO suite of simulations was employed to compare heating mechanisms: star-forming clumps vs. a major merger in a Milky Way analog.
AI.result: Only clumpy Milky Way models produced both high-α and low-α Splash populations via scattering by early clumps; the merger-only model (without an early clumpy phase) failed to produce these populations.
AI.conclusion: The low-α Splash is a subset of the old thin disk dynamically heated by the same mechanism responsible for the high-α Splash, supporting clump-driven heating rather than merger-driven heating as the origin.

title: Kinematic hints of a nuclear bar in the Milky Way
summary: The Milky Way hosts a flattened nuclear stellar disc (NSD) that dominates the gravitational potential in the inner few hundred parsecs. Whether the NSD is purely axisymmetric or contains a nuclear bar remains an open question. We test for the presence of a nuclear bar using kinematic diagnostics by combining line-of-sight velocities from the KMOS NSD survey with proper motions from VIRAC2 to construct the $ (v_\ell, v_\mathrm{los}) $ velocity ellipse. After applying strict quality cuts to minimise contamination from large-scale bar stars, we measure the vertex deviation $ l_v $ and anisotropy $ β$ for several subsamples. For our primary sample ($ |\ell| < 0.9^\circ $, $ -0.4^\circ < b < 0.25^\circ $, $ \mathrm{[Fe/H]} > -0.3 $), we find a significant negative vertex deviation $ l_v = -54.8^{+13.1}_{-14.8}\,^\circ $ with moderate anisotropy $ β= 0.16^{+0.08}_{-0.05} $. A subsample restricted to the innermost four fields yields an even stronger signal with $ l_v = -64.3^{+12.1}_{-12.2}\,^\circ $ and $ β= 0.38^{+0.12}_{-0.07} $. The direction of maximum velocity dispersion is oriented along Galactic longitude, opposite to that observed in large-scale bar-dominated samples. These signatures are robust against extinction-driven incompleteness, primary-bar contamination, and the choice of metallicity threshold. They are inconsistent with an axisymmetric NSD or one oriented orthogonally to the primary bar, but match expectations for a nuclear bar oriented at $ α\approx 60^\circ $-$75^\circ$ to the Sun-Galactic-Centre line with its near side pointing toward positive Galactic longitude. While definitive confirmation awaits larger and more precise samples from upcoming surveys, our results provide the first kinematic indication of a possible nuclear bar in the Milky Way.

AI.tldr: Using combined line-of-sight velocities and proper motions, this paper finds the first kinematic evidence for a nuclear bar in the Milky Way's nuclear stellar disc, characterized by a significant negative vertex deviation (lv = -54.8°) and anisotropy (β = 0.16), consistent with a bar oriented at ~60°–75° to the Sun-Galactic-Centre line.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the Milky Way's nuclear stellar disc (NSD) is purely axisymmetric or contains a nuclear bar, an open question in Galactic structure.
AI.method: Combined KMOS NSD survey line-of-sight velocities with VIRAC2 proper motions to construct (vℓ, vlos) velocity ellipses; applied quality cuts to minimize contamination from large-scale bar stars; measured vertex deviation lv and anisotropy β for multiple subsamples with varying metallicity and spatial constraints.
AI.result: Significant negative vertex deviation lv = -54.8° (primary sample) and -64.3° (inner fields) with moderate anisotropy; maximum velocity dispersion oriented along Galactic longitude, opposite to bar-dominated samples; signatures robust against extinction, contamination, and metallicity thresholds; consistent with a nuclear bar at α ≈ 60°–75° orientation.
AI.conclusion: The results provide the first kinematic indication of a possible nuclear bar in the Milky Way, inconsistent with an axisymmetric NSD or one orthogonal to the primary bar; definitive confirmation awaits larger, more precise surveys.

title: Simulations of gas inflow in the Milky Way I. Stellar-Feedback-Regulated Transport from the Central Molecular Zone to the Circumnuclear disk
summary: We perform hydrodynamical simulations with radially varying resolution to study the effects of stellar feedback on the radial inflow of gas from the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ, $R\sim200$ pc) to the Circumnuclear Disk (CND, $R\sim5$ pc) of the Milky Way. The simulations include a realistic Milky Way barred gravitational potential, a cooling function coupled to a non-equilibrium chemical network, gas self-gravity, star formation, supernova feedback, and radiation feedback from massive stars computed via on-the-fly radiative transfer. Our main findings are as follows: 1) Stellar feedback drives a radial inflow that decreases monotonically with decreasing Galactocentric radius. The time-averaged inflow rate in our fiducial SNRad simulation, which includes both supernova and radiation feedback, declines from $\langle \dot{M} \rangle\sim5\times10^{-3}$ Msun/yr at $R\sim100$ pc, to $\langle\dot{M}\rangle\sim10^{-4}$ Msun/yr at $R\sim10$ pc, to $\langle\dot{M}\rangle\sim10^{-6}$ Msun/yr at $R\sim1$ pc. 2) The total inflow rate can be broken down into two components driven by two distinct mechanisms. First, feedback-driven turbulence redistributes the angular momentum of gas clouds, producing a smooth (secular) transport of mass inward, similar to a Shakura-Sunyaev viscous accretion disk. This component contributes inflow rates that vary from $\dot{M}\sim5\times10^{-4}$ Msun/yr at $R\sim100$ pc to $\dot{M}\sim10^{-7}$ Msun/yr at $R\sim1$ pc. Second, episodic inflow events can transiently increase the inflow rate by several orders of magnitude, reaching $\dot{M}\sim10^{-3}$ Msun/yr over timescales of $Δt\sim3$-$5$ Myr at $R=10$ pc. 3) The stellar feedback model significantly affects the episodic inflow but has little impact on the smooth component. Simulations including radiation feedback produce substantially more episodic events than those with supernova feedback alone.

AI.tldr: Hydrodynamic simulations of Milky Way's CMZ-to-CND gas inflow show stellar feedback drives radial inflow via two components: a smooth, viscous-like secular transport (10^-7-5×10^-4 Msun/yr) and episodic inflow events (up to 10^-3 Msun/yr over 3-5 Myr). Radiation feedback enhances episodic events more than supernova feedback alone.
AI.motivation: To understand how stellar feedback regulates gas inflow from the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ, ~200 pc) to the Circumnuclear Disk (CND, ~5 pc), which governs the gas supply to the supermassive black hole at the Galactic center.
AI.method: Hydrodynamical simulations with radially varying resolution, including a realistic Milky Way barred gravitational potential, non-equilibrium chemical network cooling, gas self-gravity, star formation, supernova feedback, and on-the-fly radiative transfer from massive stars.
AI.result: 1) Inflow rate decreases monotonically with radius (5×10^-3 Msun/yr at 100 pc → 10^-6 Msun/yr at 1 pc). 2) Inflow has two components: smooth secular transport via turbulence-driven angular momentum redistribution (10^-7-5×10^-4 Msun/yr) and episodic events (up to 10^-3 Msun/yr for 3-5 Myr). 3) Radiation feedback substantially enhances episodic inflow compared to supernova feedback alone, while the smooth component is insensitive to feedback model.
AI.conclusion: Stellar feedback drives gas inflow toward the Galactic center through a combination of steady turbulent transport and episodic bursts, with radiation feedback being the primary driver of the transient, high-rate inflow events.

title: No Stream Left Unscathed: The imprint of a host galaxy
comment: 34 pages, 24 figures, submitted to APJ. Comments are welcome!
summary: Stellar streams from disrupted globular clusters are excellent probes of dark matter (DM) subhalos. Observed Milky Way streams display a remarkable diversity of features: spurs, gaps, kinks, cocoons, and density variations, many attributed to subhalo encounters. But how much of this diversity arises from the host itself? We simulate $\sim$15,000 globular cluster streams across four Milky Way-mass halos from the FIRE-2 cosmological simulations, evolved in basis function expansion potentials capturing the evolving disk, halo, and large-scale structure while excluding small-scale perturbers such as DM subhalos and giant molecular clouds. We find that roughly three quarters of streams develop complex features from the host potential, such as spurs, kinks, and cocoon-like envelopes. Even the smoothest streams exhibit 10--25\% width variation along their track and host overdensities and gaps at scales of ${\sim}2^\circ$, squarely in the $1^\circ$--$5^\circ$ range predicted for subhalo-induced gaps. Pericentric distance is the primary predictor of stream morphology, with ${\sim}15$ kpc separating smooth from disturbed streams and circular orbits beyond $\sim$20 kpc producing the smoothest streams. Only $\sim$70 out of $\sim$15,000 streams are free of detectable wiggles in the track at any scale. Analogs to observed features, such as the GD-1 spur and the ATLAS--Aliqa Uma kink, emerge even without the presence of subhalos. As next-generation surveys (LSST, Euclid, and Roman) resolve stream structure across hundreds of streams, the baseline established here, streams evolved without small-scale perturbers, becomes essential for extracting DM substructure constraints.

AI.tldr: Simulations of ~15,000 globular cluster streams in FIRE-2 Milky Way-mass halos (without subhalos) show that ~75% develop complex morphological features (spurs, kinks, cocoons) from the host potential alone, challenging the assumption that such features uniquely trace dark matter subhalo encounters.
AI.motivation: Stellar streams are used as probes of dark matter subhalos, but the observed diversity of stream features (spurs, gaps, kinks, cocoons) may be partially or largely caused by the host potential rather than subhalo encounters. This paper aims to quantify how much stream complexity arises from the host galaxy itself.
AI.method: ~15,000 globular cluster streams are simulated across four Milky Way-mass halos from FIRE-2 cosmological simulations, using basis function expansion potentials that capture the evolving disk, halo, and large-scale structure but exclude small-scale perturbers (DM subhalos, giant molecular clouds). Stream morphology is analyzed statistically.
AI.result: ~75% of streams develop complex features from the host potential alone. Even smoothest streams show 10–25% width variation and host overdensities/gaps at ~2° scales (within 1°–5° range predicted for subhalo-induced gaps). Pericentric distance is the primary predictor; ~15 kpc separates smooth from disturbed streams. Only ~70/15,000 streams are free of detectable track wiggles. Observed features like GD-1 spur and ATLAS–Aliqa Uma kink appear without subhalos.
AI.conclusion: The host potential alone produces a rich diversity of stream morphology, so observed stream features cannot be uniquely attributed to dark matter subhalos. This baseline (streams without small-scale perturbers) is essential for extracting DM substructure constraints from next-generation surveys (LSST, Euclid, Roman).
